parts: Reproduction is the biological process by which organisms give rise to their own kind, so that a species continues from one generation to the next. In asexual reproduction a single individual produces offspring; in sexual reproduction a male gamete fuses with a female gamete to begin a new individual.

Binary fission: a cell divides into two and loses its own identity (Amoeba, bacteria). Budding: a bud grows on the parent and later separates (yeast; in multicellular Hydra and sponges the bud forms all body parts before detaching). Spore formation: the nucleus and cytoplasm divide repeatedly into spores that grow into new individuals (Chlamydomonas, fungi, moss, fern).

Vegetative propagation is asexual reproduction in plants from roots, stems or leaves. Natural methods: adventitious roots (sweet potato, dahlia); runner (lawn grass); sucker (chrysanthemum); bulb (onion); tuber (potato); rhizome (ginger); adventitious buds on leaf edges (Bryophyllum). Artificial methods used by farmers and nurseries: cutting (rose, money plant), layering (jasmine, grapevine), gootee (air layering) and grafting (citrus, mango), where a scion is joined to a stock. Banana plants that are genetically similar are grown by vegetative propagation.

Micropropagation (tissue culture): every plant cell is totipotent, so a piece of tissue in a nutrient medium forms an undifferentiated mass, the callus, which with hormones grows into plantlets. Cloning: a clone is a genetic copy of the parent; Dolly the sheep was made by putting the nucleus of her mother's udder cell into an egg (of a surrogate mother) whose nucleus had been removed.

The flower is the reproductive organ. The stamens (androecium) are the male part — each has an anther, which produces pollen, held on a filament. The pistil (gynoecium) is the female part — stigma, style and ovary, which contains the ovules. Bisexual flowers have both; unisexual flowers have one. Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma by wind, water or insects: self-pollination is to the stigma of the same flower; cross-pollination is to a flower of another plant of the same species. On the stigma each pollen grain grows a pollen tube through the style to the ovule, and the male nucleus fuses with the egg (fertilisation). Fertilised ovules become seeds, the ovary becomes the fruit, and seeds germinate into new plants.

The female produces eggs and the male sperms; they fuse to form a zygote which develops into an embryo. Oviparous animals lay eggs (fish, frogs, reptiles, birds); viviparous animals give birth to young that develop in the mother's womb (cats, cows, humans). Hermaphrodites have both male and female organs in one individual (earthworm, tapeworm).

Adolescence (about 10–19 years) is the stage of physical, physiological and psychological change between childhood and adulthood; puberty is the period when the body becomes capable of reproduction. Changes: growth spurt, more active sweat and oil glands (acne), greater appetite, rise of growth hormone and sex hormones (testosterone from testes; oestrogen and progesterone from ovaries, under control of pituitary hormones), secondary sexual characters (body hair, breasts in girls, facial hair and deeper voice in boys), and mood swings and self-consciousness. The first menstruation is menarche; its stopping at 45–55 years is menopause.

Menstrual cycle: about every 28 days an ovum matures (under FSH) and is released; the uterine wall thickens (under LH) to receive a fertilised egg. If fertilisation does not happen, the lining and blood vessels break down and are shed as menstruation. Adolescent pregnancy is harmful to mother and child; the legal age at marriage is 18 for girls and 21 for boys.

Male: a pair of testes (produce sperms and testosterone; kept in the scrotum about 2 °C below body temperature), two vasa deferentia (sperm ducts), which join to form the ejaculatory duct, and the penis. Female: a pair of ovaries (produce ova and hormones), two fallopian tubes (oviducts, where fertilisation takes place), the uterus or womb (where the embryo develops), the cervix (opening of the uterus) and the vagina.

A sperm (head, middle piece, tail) fuses with the ovum in the fallopian tube to form the zygote. It divides into a ball of cells that becomes embedded (implanted) in the thickened uterine wall; the embryo, now a foetus, develops for about 280 days and is born under the influence of oxytocin from the posterior pituitary.

Planning family size and the timing of births improves quality of life. Temporary methods: condoms and diaphragms (barriers that stop sperm meeting the egg), IUCD such as Copper-T (prevents implantation), oral pills (stop ovulation). Permanent methods: vasectomy in males (vas deferens tied) and tubectomy in females (fallopian tubes blocked).

Reproductive tract infections come from poor genital hygiene; those spread by sexual contact are sexually transmitted diseases — gonorrhoea, syphilis, herpes, chlamydia, warts, chancroid. Symptoms include itching, sores, abnormal discharge and pain on urination; untreated STDs can cause infertility. HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus, an RNA retrovirus) destroys T-helper lymphocytes and leads to AIDS (Acquired Immuno-Deficiency Syndrome). It spreads by unprotected sex, infected blood, shared needles and from an infected mother to her baby; it does not spread by touching, hugging, sharing food or toilets, coughing or mosquitoes. Prevention: one faithful partner, correct use of condoms, sterilised needles and screened blood.
